analysis.one_liner: Caps punitive damage awards in federal and state courts at the greater of three times actual losses or $250,000.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap punitive damages in most financial-injury cases at the greater of $250,000 or three times actual losses was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got one hearing in July 1998, and died without ever receiving a vote before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have capped punitive damages — extra money juries award to punish wrongdoing — in civil cases involving financial injury, such as fraud, insurance disputes, or deceptive business practices. The cap would be the greater of $250,000 or three times the person's actual monetary losses, with a lower cap (the lesser of the two) for small businesses, individuals worth under $500,000, and local governments. It would apply even in state courts, and juries would not be told the cap exists. Cases involving death or serious physical injury, and defendants convicted of violent, hate, or sexual offenses or acting while drunk or on illegal drugs, would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations, insurers, and small businesses that face or pay punitive damage awards in financial-injury lawsuits would gain a predictable ceiling on their exposure. The bill's own findings argue this would reduce awards by up to 40%, lower liability insurance costs, and keep products and services from being withdrawn from the market because of unpredictable verdicts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporate defendants, insurers, and small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Caps punitive damages in covered financial-injury cases at the greater of three times economic loss or $250,000, giving corporate defendants and their insurers a predictable maximum exposure in both federal and state courts.
Gives small businesses, individuals with net worth under $500,000, and local governments an even lower cap — the lesser of three times economic loss or $250,000 — when they are defendants.

Cites a Rand Institute study claiming the cap would reduce grossly excessive punitive awards by as much as 40%, lower prices, and address the Supreme Court's concern in BMW v. Gore about awards grossly out of proportion to the harm.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, investors, and policyholders who win lawsuits over financial wrongdoing would collect less, because the punitive damages meant to punish and deter fraud or bad faith would be capped — and the jury deciding their case would never be told the cap exists. States would also lose control over their own damage rules in any covered case affecting interstate commerce.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers and investors suing over financial harm

drawbacks.text: The cap would have applied in state courts, overriding each state's own damage rules in nearly any commercial dispute, since the bill defines 'interstate commerce' broadly enough to cover most business-related cases.

A wronged customer, investor, or employee would be limited to $250,000 in punitive damages no matter how large the company or how egregious the misconduct, and the jury would never know the cap had been applied.

The only escape from the cap required a criminal conviction for a violent, hate, or sexual offense, terrorism, or proof the defendant was drunk or on illegal drugs at the time — carve-outs that would rarely apply to corporate fraud or insurance bad faith.
The bill would have applied to lawsuits filed after its enactment even when the harmful conduct happened years earlier, changing the rules after the fact for pending disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — predictable liability, potentially lower insurance costs and prices — flow mainly to corporate defendants and insurers, and nothing in the bill guarantees those savings reach consumers. The costs fall on people harmed by financial misconduct, who would lose the punitive damages that punish and deter fraud, and on states, whose own damage laws would be supplanted. The bill's supporting evidence was a single Rand study cited in its own findings; the question of whether caps would actually lower prices or simply let wrongdoers off cheap was never tested, because the bill never got a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee after a July 1998 hearing; no committee or floor vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on November 13, 1997, joined by Senator Joseph Lieberman, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which Hatch chaired.
The only action after referral was a Judiciary Committee hearing on July 29, 1998; the bill was never reported out of committee or brought to the Senate floor.
No vote was ever taken in either chamber before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, so the cap never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers, investors, and others who sue over financial wrongdoing are better off, because they kept their full state-law remedies and juries can still award uncapped punitive damages against companies that commit fraud. Corporate defendants and insurers did not get the liability ceiling they sought.

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.role: Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and used his committee to hold its only hearing, in July 1998, but never brought it to a committee vote or the floor.

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's Democratic cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Business and insurance groups backing federal tort reform
for.what_they_did: Pushed Congress throughout the 1990s for federal caps on punitive damage awards in state courts.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for Senate action after its committee hearing; no floor vote ever occurred.

against.name: Trial lawyers (plaintiffs' bar)
against.what_they_did: Fought federal damage caps throughout the 1990s tort-reform debates as cuts to injured consumers' compensation.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never measured; sponsorship was bipartisan, with a Republican sponsor and two cosponsors split one Democrat and one Republican.

industries.note: The cap would directly reduce what insurers and corporations pay in punitive awards and would shrink settlements through what the bill's own findings call the 'shadow effect' of damage caps. For consumers, that means less compensation and less deterrence when companies commit fraud or bad faith.
The bill gives them a lower cap — the lesser of three times economic loss or $250,000 — when they are defendants, shielding them from large verdicts at the expense of people they injure financially.
Caps on punitive awards shrink recoveries and contingency fees in financial-injury cases, which is why plaintiffs' lawyers led opposition to federal damage caps.
